**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me he was leaving. He sat at the kitchen table, hands wrapped around a chipped mug of coffee gone cold, and said, *"I can’t do this anymore."* Just five words, but they pressed down on my chest like a stack of encyclopedias. I was eight. I didn’t know then that some sentences are boulders, that they roll into your life and crush the landscape of what you thought was permanent.

Words are supposed to be light, aren’t they? They float in the air, dissipate like breath on a winter morning. But the heavy ones linger. They settle in your bones. *"You’re not enough."* *"I don’t love you anymore."* *"It’s cancer."* Three syllables can collapse a universe.

II.

I once read that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. That’s 16,000 opportunities to build or destroy, to mend or wound. Most of them are forgettable—*"Pass the salt," "What time is it?"*—but some stick like burrs. My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Holloway, told me my stories were *"too strange for a child."* I stopped writing for seven years.

Now, I write every day. Not because I have something profound to say, but because I’m afraid of the silence. Silence is where the heavy words fester. It’s where *"I should have"* and *"If only"* grow fat and hungry. So I fill the page with noise, with metaphors and half-truths, with the detritus of a mind that won’t shut up.

III.

There’s a myth that writers are born with a surplus of words, that we’re overflowing vessels of language just waiting to spill onto the page. But the truth is, most of us are hoarders. We collect words like squirrels collect acorns—one for joy, one for grief, one for the way the light slants through the blinds at 3 PM in November. We tuck them away, afraid we’ll run out.

I have a notebook where I write down words I love. *"Petrichor."* *"Saudade."* *"Limerence."* They’re like tiny spells. Saying them feels like touching something sacred. But the words I fear are the ones I don’t write down. The ones that live in the back of my throat, sharp as fishhooks. *"I’m lonely."* *"I don’t know what I’m doing."* *"Help."*

IV.

My grandmother used to say, *"Words are free, but they cost everything."* She was a woman who measured her speech like flour in a recipe—precise, never wasteful. When she called me *"a good girl"* (her highest praise), it meant more than a thousand *"I love yous"* from someone else.

I think about her now, when I scroll through the endless chatter of the internet. Words thrown around like confetti, meaningless in their abundance. *"This is iconic."* *"I can’t even."* *"Slay."* We drown in them. We say so much that we say nothing at all.

V.

There’s a Japanese concept called *"kotodama"*—the idea that words have a soul, that they can alter reality. That’s why curses work in fairy tales. That’s why *"I do"* changes your life. That’s why *"You’re fired"* can make a man weep in a parking lot.

I believe in kotodama. I believe that the words we speak into the mirror at 2 AM, the ones we whisper to our pets, the ones we scream into pillows—they shape us. They carve grooves into our brains, deepen with each repetition. *"I’m stupid."* *"No one will ever love me."* *"I’ll never be happy."* Say them enough, and they become true.

VI.

I have a friend who is a poet. She tells me that the best poems are the ones that feel like a punch to the gut. Not because they’re violent, but because they’re *true*. A single line can steal your breath. *"Do you ever just put your hand to your chest and feel the terror of your own heartbeat?"* She wrote that once. I still haven’t recovered.

Truth is the heaviest word of all.

VII.

I’m thinking about the words I’ve swallowed. The ones that lodged in my throat like stones. The *"I’m sorry"* I didn’t say to my mother before she died. The *"I love you"* I couldn’t admit to my best friend, who moved across the country and never came back. The *"I’m scared"* that lives in my ribs, a constant hum.

What would happen if I spat them all out? Would the world tilt? Would the sky crack open?

VIII.

Here’s what I know: Words can be weapons. They can be balm. They can be both at once. *"This will hurt me more than it hurts you."* A lie and a comfort. A knife and a bandage.

I’ve been cut by words. I’ve been stitched up by them, too.

IX.

I have 1000 words. I’ve used 600. What do I do with the rest?

Maybe I’ll tell you about the time I found a love letter in a library book. It was tucked between pages 47 and 48 of *Wuthering Heights*, written in looping cursive on the back of a grocery receipt. *"I think about you when the rain hits the window like this. Like tiny fingers tapping out Morse code. I don’t know what you’re saying, but I’m listening."* I kept it. I still have it. Some words are too beautiful to leave behind.

Maybe I’ll confess that I’m terrified of silence. That I fill my days with podcasts and audiobooks and music because the absence of words feels like the absence of air. That I talk to myself in the car, in the shower, in the dark. That I’m not sure if I’m keeping the loneliness at bay or just giving it a voice.

Maybe I’ll admit that I don’t know how to end this. That all my life, I’ve been better at beginnings. That I start essays and stories and relationships with fiery enthusiasm, only to fizzle out when the last page comes. That I’m afraid of *"The End"* because it feels so final, so heavy.

X.

Here’s the truth: I don’t have a grand conclusion. No neat bow to tie this up with. Just this—words are all we have. They’re how we reach across the void, how we say *"I’m here, I’m here, I’m here."* They’re how we lie, how we love, how we pretend we’re not afraid.

So I’ll keep writing. Even when it’s hard. Even when the words feel like lead. Because the alternative—silence—is worse.

And if you’re reading this, know that you’re not alone in the weight of it all. Know that someone, somewhere, is also pressing their hand to their chest, feeling the terror of their own heartbeat, and whispering: *"Me too."*
